clock_meridiem_am: Postposed morning daypart words that keep a bare 12-hour clock reading in
the AM half (meridiem offset 0), the am counterpart of
clock_meridiem_pm.voc.  "klokken ni om formiddagen" == 09:00; only the noon
edge is rewritten (12 -> 0).  Bands: Unicode CLDR 47 Day Period Rules,
locale da -- morgen [05:00, 10:00) and formiddag [10:00, 12:00) are the am
half.  ("natten" is NOT here: the night daypart crosses midnight -- see
clock_meridiem_night: The NIGHT daypart is a midnight-crossing BAND, not the morning/night AM
half it was previously grouped in: "klokken tre om natten" (three at night)
is 03:00 but "klokken elleve om natten" (eleven at night) is 23:00, and
twelve is midnight 00:00.  Small hours 1..5 stay AM, late-night hours 6..11
are PM, twelve is midnight (the band-split lives in the resolver
_clock_hms).  The AM ceiling follows the CLDR da nat band [00:00, 05:00)
clock_meridiem_pm: Postposed daypart words that put a bare 12-hour clock reading into the
afternoon/evening half (meridiem offset +12), exactly as the de locale's
"nachmittags"/"abends" already do.  Danish trails these definite surfaces
after the "om" particle ("kvart over tre om eftermiddagen" == 15:15,
Bands: Unicode CLDR 47 Day Period Rules, locale da -- eftermiddag
[12:00, 18:00) and aften [18:00, 24:00) are the pm half.
daypart_aften_da: Band boundaries: Unicode CLDR 47 Day Period Rules, locale da
which gives formiddag as "den del af dagen der ligger mellem morgen og
middag, ca. mellem kl. 9 og 12". The dictionary's approximate 9 is the
chart's 10; the chart is followed, being the machine-readable source
every other language here is transcribed from.

daypart_morgen_da: Band boundaries: Unicode CLDR 47 Day Period Rules, locale da
Only the DEFINITE form ships here, deliberately excluding the bare
"morgen" that sibling dayparts (aften/aftenen, nat/natten) both ship --
bare "morgen" is the relative-day word for "tomorrow" ("i morgen"), and
registering it as a daypart surface too would collide with that reading
on every sentence. "morgenen" never appears in the tomorrow idiom ("i
morgen" is always the bare form), so it carries no such ambiguity. The
same surface is already used safely as a meridiem marker in
